strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple models (LLaVA-1.5 7B/13B, Qwen2-VL 7B) and hallucination-focused benchmarks (POPE, CHAIR, MMHal-Bench) with general vision-language tasks (MME, SEED-Bench)
Consistent and substantial improvements on hallucination metrics (20.7% on CHAIR, 15.9% on MMHal-Bench) while maintaining general performance
Well-motivated identification of three specific limitations in prior work: visual attention sink, low visual contribution, and cross-modal fusion imbalance
Strong ablation studies (Table 4) validating that both visual enhancement and cross-modal balance components are essential
Low computational overhead (1.13× vs. greedy decoding) with clear latency benchmarking
Quantitative saliency map validation (Table 1) showing 2.2× improvement of shift method over static baseline
Good reproducibility support with detailed implementation details, hyperparameter tuning methodology, and honest limitations discussion
weaknesses: Limited novelty: combines established techniques (attention steering via bias injection from Zhang et al. 2023, saliency-based attention guidance from recent work) without significant methodological innovation

Critical unresolved query dependency: method relies on POS tagging for information-rich words, failing on vague/visually-irrelevant/multilingual queries; paper acknowledges but provides no solutions or empirical failure rate analysis

Insufficient layer selection justification: saliency map layer chosen based on only 50 TextVQA examples then applied across different datasets (POPE, CHAIR) without validation; cross-dataset generalization not established
Cross-modal balance coefficient β=1.0 not empirically validated: paper acknowledges 'investigating whether this balance is truly optimal is left for future work,' yet this is a core design choice

Limited direct evaluation of attention sink mitigation: Table 1 evaluates saliency on COCO single-instance objects (non-representative of hallucination), without direct measurement of reduced attention to irrelevant regions during generation
No statistical significance testing despite potential variance in GPT-4.1 scoring (which requires averaging 5 runs); no confidence intervals or p-values provided
Incomplete ablation studies: no justification for top 50% attention head selection, min-max normalization choice, or three standard deviation clipping threshold
Modest improvements on some benchmarks: POPE F1 improvement is only 3.0% (86.0→86.8), limiting practical significance; 13% computational overhead may be problematic for real-time applications
Insufficient generalization analysis: only tested on 7B/13B models with model-specific hyperparameters (α=5.0 vs 4.0); no evaluation on newer models or other architectures
Limited failure mode analysis: Figure 12 shows residual hallucinations but provides no systematic error analysis or breakdown by hallucination type; no comparison of when/why GIFT fails vs baselines

strengths: Clear problem formulation identifying three concrete limitations in prior hallucination mitigation methods (attention sink, low visual contribution, imbalanced cross-modal fusion)
Intuitive core idea of using positive attention shifts instead of absolute attention scores, validated empirically (Table 1: saliency score 11.92 vs. 5.40)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple architectures (LLaVA-1.5 7B/13B, Qwen2-VL) and diverse benchmarks (CHAIR, POPE, MMHal-Bench, SEED-Bench, MME)
Principled approach to cross-modal balance by scaling query attention proportionally to visual enhancement (Eq. 7), supported by attention pattern analysis (Figure 4)
Practical computational efficiency with only 1.13x latency overhead compared to baselines
Honest discussion of limitations, particularly regarding query-dependency and heavy reliance on query quality
Ablation studies (Table 4) demonstrating that both visual enhancement and query balancing components are necessary
weaknesses: Limited novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (attention steering from Zhang et al. 2023, standard visual saliency mapping) with incremental refinement of using attention shifts instead of absolute attention and adding query adjustment
Weak theoretical justification: lacks rigorous explanation for why positive attention shifts specifically mitigate attention sink problems, or why min-max normalization with 3-std clipping is optimal

Critical methodological flaw: uses 10% of test benchmarks (POPE and MME) as 'pseudo-validation' sets for hyperparameter tuning, then tests on remaining 90%, effectively overfitting to specific benchmarks
Insufficient sample size for layer selection: uses only 50 TextVQA examples to select critical hyperparameters (saliency computation layer, enhancement layers), risking poor generalization

Incomplete baseline comparisons: for Qwen2-VL 7B, only compares against greedy decoding because other baseline implementations unavailable, preventing assessment of relative effectiveness on this architecture

Query dependency inadequately analyzed: acknowledges that vague/ambiguous/visually-irrelevant queries reduce effectiveness but provides no empirical analysis of performance degradation, query type breakdowns, or failure modes

Multiple heuristic design choices without ablation: 50% head selection threshold, spaCy POS tagging for information-rich words, specific normalization approaches all lack justification or sensitivity analysis
Mixed results on general reasoning tasks: Table 3 shows negative or comparable performance on MME for LLaVA-1.5 7B (1750.5 vs. 1751.6), contradicting claim of minimal impact on reasoning capabilities
Limited error analysis: Figure 12 shows failure case but provides minimal systematic analysis of hallucination types GIFT addresses best or worst, or false positive rates

Evaluation unreliability: GPT-4.1 scoring for MMHal-Bench requires 5 runs due to inherent randomness, and only 96 examples in benchmark is quite small; relying on GPT-4 as ground truth introduces potential biases
Incomplete ablations: Table 4 doesn't isolate gaze shift saliency computation contribution from cross-modal balancing; no comparison against alternative saliency computation methods
Scalability concerns: experiments limited to 7B/13B models; performance on larger models unknown; method adds latency per query, limiting applicability for high-throughput scenarios
Missing analysis of cross-modal balance: sets β=1.0 to preserve balance but provides no justification, ablation, or analysis of sensitivity to this hyperparameter choice

strengths: Clear motivation addressing three specific limitations of prior work: visual attention sink, low visual contribution, and imbalanced cross-modal fusion, with concrete examples
Novel insight about preserving cross-modal balance by scaling query token attention proportionally to visual enhancement (Eq. 7), well-validated through ablations

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple VLM architectures (LLaVA 7B/13B, Qwen2-VL), multiple hallucination benchmarks (CHAIR, POPE, MMHal-Bench), and general reasoning tasks (SEED-Bench, MME)
Consistent improvements across all tested configurations, with substantial gains on CHAIR (up to 20.7%) and MMHal-Bench (15.9%)
Excellent computational efficiency: 1.13× latency vs. greedy decoding compared to 11.10× for VAR and 1.56× for Rel-Attn
Strong ablation studies (Table 4) demonstrating that both visual and query attention enhancement are essential for performance
Well-written with clear presentation, effective visualizations (especially Figure 1 comparing static vs. shift saliency maps), and honest discussion of limitations
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: attention steering via saliency maps is standard; the main contribution is computing saliency maps via positive shifts rather than static averaging, which is an incremental improvement

Heavy dependency on query quality largely unexplored: relies on heuristic POS tagging to identify information-rich tokens; no systematic evaluation of performance degradation with vague, ambiguous, or non-English queries
Modest improvements on some benchmarks: POPE shows only 3.0% improvement (82.4→83.8 F1) and SEED-Bench shows 0.1-0.2% improvement, potentially within noise without statistical significance testing

Reproducibility concerns: MMHal-Bench evaluation shifted to GPT-4.1 due to GPT-4 deprecation with 5-run averaging due to randomness; Qwen2-VL baseline results unavailable, only compared with greedy decoding

Insufficient justification of key design choices: (1) Why track only positive shifts rather than absolute changes? (2) Why top 50% head selection? (3) Why is β=1.0 optimal? Authors acknowledge this is left for future work. (4) Different layers selected for different models without generalization analysis
Limited sample for layer selection: only 50 TextVQA examples used to identify optimal layers for saliency map computation and cross-modal fusion
Lack of statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests; no error analysis identifying which query/image types the method fails on
Theoretical grounding weak: the connection to human visual attention is intuitive but superficial; no principled explanation for why tracking positive shifts should outperform alternatives

strengths: Clear problem motivation with well-articulated limitations of prior work (attention sink, low visual contribution, imbalanced cross-modal fusion)
Novel gaze shift-based saliency map computation that empirically demonstrates 2.2× improvement over static attention (Table 1) and naturally mitigates attention sink
Addresses important cross-modal fusion balance by proportionally scaling query attention based on visual enhancement (Eq. 7), distinguishing from VAF/VAR
Comprehensive experiments across 4 model architectures, 7 benchmarks, with thorough ablations demonstrating component contributions (up to 25.4% improvement from joint components vs. visual-only)
Strong empirical results: 20.7% improvement on CHAIR, 15.9% on MMHal-Bench, consistent gains across diverse models
Practical efficiency with only 1.13× latency overhead compared to 1.56-11.10× for baselines
Layer selection robustness demonstrated: multiple moderate layer configurations achieve strong performance (Table 6)
Clear presentation with effective visualizations, well-organized appendices, and honest limitations discussion
Works across multiple VLM architectures (LLaVA-1.5, Qwen) without retraining, enabling practical deployment
weaknesses: Limited novelty: attention steering is established; main contribution is saliency map preprocessing; cross-modal balance adjustment is straightforward extension

Significant unresolved limitation: method depends on query tokens to identify visual regions; fails when answers don't require visual information or queries are irrelevant to images; acknowledged but not addressed with default implementation

Inconsistent improvements across metrics: POPE shows only 3.0% improvement vs. 20.7% on CHAIR, suggesting method works better for some hallucination types than others with no analysis of which categories benefit

Overclaimed 'intrinsic' layer selection: tested on only 50 examples, 2 datasets (both visual understanding); different models show different peak layers (11, 10, 14, 18) contradicting universality claim

Insufficient justification for key design choices: exponential scaling in Eq. 6 (why not linear?), clipping at 3σ (no ablation), β fixed to 1.0 ('investigating optimality left for future work' contradicts principled design claims)
Weak statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or error bars; GPT-4.1 scoring variance unreported; Figure 6 shows performance oscillations
Suboptimal default word extraction: POS tagging selected over LLM-based approach despite Table 7 showing better results (52.6 vs 57.3), justified only by 'negligible overhead'
Limited failure analysis: Figure 12 shows remaining hallucinations but no systematic error categorization; missing analysis of when method helps most/least

Metric reliability concerns inadequately addressed: authors acknowledge CHAIR may misrepresent Qwen3-VL 8B's hallucinations as string-matching artifact, yet headline results still emphasize CHAIR gains
Baseline comparison limited: VAF, Rel-Attn, VCD, VAR only on LLaVA-1.5; no Qwen2/3 comparisons for these methods; insufficient implementation details for reproducibility

strengths: Addresses an important problem (VLM hallucinations) with consistent empirical improvements across multiple models (LLaVA, Qwen) and hallucination benchmarks
Low computational overhead (1.13× vs greedy decoding) compared to other baselines (1.56-11.10×), making the method practical
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including extensive ablation studies (Tables 5-7) that validate component contributions
Intuitive core insight: tracking positive attention shifts to identify task-relevant regions naturally mitigates visual attention sink without explicit filtering
Clear presentation with good visualizations (Figures 1, 3, 4) and detailed implementation details supporting reproducibility
Demonstrates robustness across layer selection (Table 6) and shows the peak layer is intrinsic to model architecture (Appendix A)
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core contribution is incremental, essentially replacing absolute attention with positive attention shifts in existing attention-steering frameworks (acknowledged prior work by Yin et al. 2025, Zhang et al. 2023)
Methodological flaw: hyperparameter tuning uses 10% of test sets (POPE/MME) as 'pseudo-validation' sets, violating train-test separation and potentially inflating reported improvements
Unfair baseline comparisons: full baseline comparisons only on LLaVA models; on Qwen models, only compared against greedy decoding, not against VAF/VAR or other methods
Modest improvements on POPE (3.0%) and no statistical significance testing despite claims of improvements 'up to 20.7%'; no error bars or confidence intervals reported

Anomalous results undermine generalizability: Qwen3-VL 8B shows degraded CHAIR performance (worse than greedy), with authors' post-hoc explanation that the model generates detailed descriptions problematic
Lack of theoretical justification: why positive attention shifts specifically capture task-relevant regions is not principled; the 'gaze shift' human vision analogy is not validated

Heavy query-dependence acknowledged but not addressed: when queries don't relate to visual content or contain irrelevant portions, the method produces inaccurate saliency maps and unnecessary visual focus

Custom evaluation metric (Table 1 normalized saliency score) is specific to object detection from bounding boxes and may not reflect performance on other hallucination types (attribute, relation hallucinations)
Missing failure analysis: no explicit characterization of when/why the method fails or works poorly, limiting understanding of method boundaries

Simplistic design choices: POS tagging for information-rich words is language-dependent; Table 7 shows LLM-based extraction outperforms it, yet default is suboptimal; β=1.0 hardcoded for all models despite different attention patterns (Figure 4)

strengths: Strong empirical results with substantial improvements across multiple benchmarks (up to 20.7% on CHAIR, 15.9% on MMHal-Bench) while maintaining general reasoning performance
Comprehensive experimental validation across 4 different VLM architectures and sizes, with thorough ablations demonstrating the importance of each component
Honest and clear presentation of limitations with practical solutions; comprehensive implementation details enabling reproducibility
Practical efficiency with only 1.13× computational overhead compared to greedy decoding, significantly better than competing methods
Well-identified problem (visual attention sink, insufficient visual contribution, cross-modal imbalance) with clear motivation for each component
Robustness demonstration across hyperparameter selection and layer choices, with stability analysis across different datasets and samples
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty - the contribution primarily combines existing techniques (visual saliency maps, attention steering, cross-modal consideration) rather than introducing fundamentally new ideas or mechanisms
Theoretical justification incomplete: rationale for tracking only positive shifts, choice of aggregation methods, and principled justification for using the peak layer lack depth

Core method dependency on query information creates limitations for cases where visual information is irrelevant or query portions are unrelated to images; no dedicated benchmark evaluates these scenarios

Design choices not fully justified: β parameter is set to 1.0 to preserve 'original balance' but optimality is acknowledged as unresolved; α differs across models but scaling relationship to model properties is underexplored

Hyperparameter tuning uses informal pseudovalidation sets (10% of benchmarks), potentially introducing benchmark-specific overfitting, and enhancement layer selection procedure could be more principled
All experiments limited to LLaVA and Qwen architectures; testing on broader set of VLM designs would strengthen generalization claims
Limited failure case analysis beyond qualitative examples; insufficient investigation of which hallucination types GIFT addresses better and propagation of incorrect saliency maps to errors
